Explore the signing mechanism
Document bytes → SHA-256 with ECDSA → signature. A private demo key creates each signature. Its corresponding public key checks the signature against the current document bytes.
A matching signature supports content integrity relative to that key. It does not prove the fictional participant is a verified person. The content fingerprint shown here is a separate diagnostic calculation.


02 / Reconstructed process map
Responsibilities, not internal infrastructure.
A new conceptual map organised around document states and decision points. The numbered stages describe this independent lab, not a former partner's deployment architecture.
01 → PREPARECompose a document
Fictional content enters the workspace. Prepare a stable text representation.
02 → FINGERPRINTIdentify the content
Calculate a hash so changes to the prepared content are visible.
03 → SIGNCollect participant signatures
Separate demo keys sign the same document bytes. Each signer records their own approval action.
04 → DECIDEVerify the current content
Check each signature against the current text and its corresponding public key.
05 → ACCEPT / REVIEWInterpret the evidence
All valid: content matches signed bytes. Failed or missing: review before treating the workflow as complete.
06 → HAND OFFExport a demo record
Download content, public keys, signatures and current verification results for inspection.
Decision branch: changed content or failed verification → review the document → explicitly prepare again → collect new signatures. Missing signatures → return to the signing room. Exporting evidence alone does not complete approval.

03 / Case study foundation
From a team prototype to a public learning lab.
A 2023 industry-sponsored graduate team project explored HTML-to-PDF generation, certificate-related services and multi-party PDF signing. This independent reconstruction explains the underlying workflow using newly written code and fictional content.
Delivery narrative
  1. Define scope. Separate document rendering, signing and certificate-related responsibilities.
  2. Research options. Explore rendering tools and signing services.
  3. Prototype and integrate. Connect the core workflow and demonstrate output.
  4. Document boundaries. Record future verification, timestamping, revocation and logging work.
Retrospective summary based on the final team report. Individual ownership and week-by-week details require further confirmation.
Public presentation boundary
Original application screens, internal code, service configuration, credentials, contact information and company documents are excluded.
The original work is presented as a team prototype. No production deployment, measured business impact or compliance certification is claimed.

Finale / from text to digital evidence
Follow the bytes. Understand the signature.
A digital document is represented by bytes. Watch a short text become UTF-8 bytes, inspect the same bytes in binary and hexadecimal, then compute a digest and create a real digital signature.
This independent example signs the entire UTF-8 text above. The full contract studio signs its structured JSON payload instead. Neither demonstration signs the bytes of an exported PDF.
Step 1 of 5
  1. Text
  2. Bytes
  3. Binary / hex
  4. SHA-256
  5. Signature
1. A document starts as content
Text is encoded into bytes before it can be stored or signed.
Text → UTF-8 bytes
Each cell below is one byte. UTF-8 characters can occupy one or more bytes.
The same bytes, two notations
OffsetBinary (base 2)Hex (base 16)
Example: 01000001₂ = 41₁₆ = byte value 65. Binary → hexadecimal only changes how the value is displayed; it is not encryption.
Digest / SHA-256
Not computed yet.
A 32-byte digest of the entire text, shown as 64 hexadecimal characters. The inspection window does not limit the hashed data.
Digital signature / ECDSA
Not created yet.
The private key signs; the public key verifies. SHA-256 is specified within the ECDSA signing call over the original bytes. We do not feed the displayed digest back into that call or sign it twice.
Reach the last step to create a signature.
Storage illustration: a drive stores encoded data using physical states managed by hardware and software. These visible 0s and 1s are a readable model of logical bits, not a scan of a real disk. Signature bytes are separate evidence, not the document converted into a signature. Identity remains a fictional demo identity.
